title: Most UNDERRATED Muscle for Aesthetics (TAKE THE NECK PILL)
summary: NH argues the neck is the most underrated aesthetic muscle: a thick neck improves the physique and facial aesthetics and may protect against concussion. He gives a cheap, adherence-focused method using plate neck curls and resistance bands in all directions, superset between main lifts, with high reps and slowly increasing weekly volume. A 17-inch neck that lines up with the jaw is enough for most people.
claims: The neck is the most underrated aesthetic muscle; a small neck makes even a great physique look bad
A thicker neck improves facial aesthetics: the jaw looks squarer and the face less fat and more masculine
A stronger, thicker neck can protect against concussions and in car crashes
The neck grows more easily during a bulk, and a muscular neck spreads fat so the face looks less like a moon face, but don't use it as an excuse to get fat
Neck training does not cause sleep apnea; overall weight gain does, and colleagues who cut back lost the snoring but kept their necks
Like calves, the neck is easy to grow but people don't stick to the training, so adherence is the real problem
Three stages: pencil neck, intermediate (aesthetic), monster; intermediate is enough, reached when the jaw lines up straight with the neck when relaxed
His neck is 17 inches and he is satisfied with it
Plates and bands are enough for an aesthetic neck; a harness or machine is only for advanced 'monster neck' goals
Progress from a 5 lb plate up to a 45 lb plate and you'll have most of the gains most people want
Superset neck sets between main lifts like squats or close-grip bench so you don't skip them, instead of leaving them for the end
The neck responds best to frequency and volume rather than intensity
Start with 3 weekly neck sets, then progress to 6, 9, then 10-12, with 10-15 or 15-20+ reps; slowing load progression is intentional
Neck injuries can be severe because of the many nerves, so prefer safe, controlled neck curls over bridges and more intense methods
Train every neck direction (flexion, extension, lateral) to avoid posture imbalances; with three neck sessions a week, train one function per day
Training neck extension also helps the back of the neck and trap look from behind
Use different weights for each neck direction, and use clean, slow 10-20 rep sets rather than heavy 3-4 rep sets
Two 45 lb plates on the head are impractical, turning into a grip exercise; beyond that invest in a harness
He finds lateral neck flexion with a plate painful and has hurt his neck doing it, so he skips it or uses bands
Bands feel more comfortable and, he believes, more hypertrophic than plates; use both for variety, to avoid overuse injuries and for adherence
Training the neck makes growing the traps easier
exercises: supine, head off bench, upper back packed; plate on the forehead close to the nose; slow controlled eccentric; chin tucked or untucked by preference
safest and most effective way to add neck size
lie on belly with upper chest at the bench edge; plate at the back of the head near the base of the skull, not on the neck; chin tucked
back of the neck, neglected, aids trap look
chin tucked, plate on the side of the head; or hand resistance as a finisher; start with very light weight
band anchored to a rack; stand and step away to increase tension; work front, back and sides; finish by stepping forward and holding
more comfortable, especially for lateral work; also hits the traps
